exp.0:0:
Obadiah presents what God showed him in a vision. The Lord speaks about Edom and says that a message has already been heard from the Lord: a messenger is sent among the nations to call them to rise up in battle against Edom. A public proclamation is what is meant by the sending of this message to the nations.

Edom was the people descended from Esau, a neighbor of Israel, and was often hostile toward it. God himself speaks through the prophet Obadiah. Very little is known about the author, and the exact date of the book is debated. The message announces judgment against Edom's pride and violence, as the following verses show.

God sees injustice, even when the powerful seem secure. Today we can examine whether we trust in our strength, our money, or our position, and remember that true security is found only in God. It also invites us to treat those who suffer with compassion, and not to rejoice in their fall.
exp.0:8:
It says that the strongest soldiers of Teman, an important city of Edom, will lose their strength. All the men of the mount of Esau will be cut down like trees by a great slaughter. The word for "cut down" is explained as meaning cut off, as trees are felled, and a great slaughter means violent destruction.

Here God speaks through the prophet Obadiah. Edom, a descendant of Esau, was a brother nation to Israel, but it rejoiced and took advantage when Jerusalem fell. Scholars do not agree on which invasion is meant, although many think of the Babylonian conquest. God announces judgment against that pride and that betrayal.

For today: do not trust your strength, your reputation, or your alliances as if they were your security. And if someone in your family suffers, do not rejoice or take advantage; help them with compassion, because God sees what we do.
exp.0:9:
It says that Edom will be covered with shame and destroyed completely, forever, because of the violence or harm it did to its brother Jacob, that is, to the people of Israel. Here "violence" means brutal treatment or harm; "cut off" means cut down or removed, as a tree is cut down.

God speaks through the prophet Obadiah. Edom, a descendant of Esau, was the brother nation of Israel, since Esau and Jacob were brothers. According to the verses that follow, Edom stood by and did nothing when strangers attacked Jerusalem, and it rejoiced over the misfortune of Judah. Scholars debate the exact moment this refers to, but God judges Edom for its lack of compassion.

For today: let us not rejoice when others are in trouble, and certainly not when they are family or brothers and sisters in the faith. If someone is suffering, let us help them, or at least stand with them with respect and compassion.
exp.0:10:
This verse reminds Edom of what it did when Jerusalem was attacked. It says that while foreigners carried off the soldiers of Judah as prisoners, entered its gates, and cast lots over the city (that is, divided it up by chance), Edom stood by, watching without helping. That is why it says Edom was like one of them. The word for "foreigners" in the verse above means people from other nations.

God speaks through the prophet Obadiah. Edom, descended from Esau, was a brother nation to Israel, descended from Jacob. God accuses them of indifference and of rejoicing at Judah's fall. Scholars often connect this to the fall of Jerusalem to Babylon, though not all agree on the exact event.

For today: do not be indifferent to the suffering of others, especially those close to us. Staying silent when we could help also counts. Today, offer a word, a prayer, or concrete help to someone who is suffering.
exp.0:11:
This verse rebukes Edom for how it acted while Judah was suffering. It says Edom should not have stood by watching with pleasure at its brother's misfortune, nor rejoiced when the children of Judah were lost, nor spoken proudly and mockingly in their day of distress. The phrase about the mouth speaking proudly describes boasting and scorn in the time of trouble. The phrase about being treated as a stranger means that Judah was treated as an outsider, carried away, or laid waste.

God speaks through the prophet Obadiah. Edom, a descendant of Esau, was a relative of Israel, a descendant of Jacob. When Jerusalem was invaded, Edom did not help and sided with the invaders. Scholars often place the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C., although they do not all agree on the exact date.

Today, when someone close to us goes through a failure or a pain, God calls us not to mock them or to feel satisfaction inwardly. We can stand with them through a prayer, a kind word, or concrete help.
exp.0:17:
This verse uses the image of a fire. The descendants of Jacob and Joseph (that is, the people of Israel) will be like fire and flame, and the descendants of Esau (Edom) will be like stubble, dry straw that burns easily. They will set them on fire and consume them, and no one will remain of Edom. All this will happen because God has spoken it.

Obadiah is a prophet who delivers God's message against Edom. Edom was a neighbor of Israel, and it rejoiced and took advantage when Jerusalem fell. God promises justice and that his people will be restored.

For today: God sees injustice and does not overlook it. We can let go of the desire for revenge, trust that he will bring justice in his time, and examine ourselves to make sure we do not rejoice in the misfortune of others.
exp.0:4:
It says that if thieves came at night to rob, they would take only what they wanted and leave the rest. Grape-pickers, when they harvest, also leave some gleanings behind. But with Edom, the destruction would be so complete that nothing would be left. The word "steal" here means to take what belongs to someone else, and the cry "oh, how you will be ruined!" expresses astonishment at the coming disaster.

God speaks through the prophet Obadiah, addressing Edom, a descendant of Esau. Edom trusted in its rock fortresses and its pride, and it mistreated Judah, its brother nation. God announces that no height will protect it from his judgment.

For today: the security we build with money, success, or position may seem firm, but it cannot save us. It is wise to trust in God, to live with humility, and to treat family and those who suffer with kindness.
exp.0:3:
Even if Edom soars as high as an eagle, or builds its nest among the stars, God himself will bring it down. No height and no hiding place, however high or secure it seems, can shield anyone from God's judgment.

God speaks through the prophet Obadiah. He addresses Edom, the people descended from Esau, who lived in rocky mountains and seemed impossible to attack. According to the context, its pride had deceived it, and it believed itself safe from any fall. God answers that its security is an illusion.

For today: Examine where you place your security, whether in money, position, or success. All of these can fail. With humility, trust in God, who is the only refuge that does not collapse.
exp.0:6:
All the men allied with you will drive you to the border. The men at peace with you will deceive and overpower you. Those who eat your bread will set a trap for you, and you will not be aware of it. It says that the very allies of Edom would drive him out of his land, pushing him all the way to the border. Those who were at peace with him would deceive and overpower him. Those who shared his table would set a trap for him. And Edom would not see the betrayal coming.

The prophet Obadiah speaks, announcing a message from the LORD against Edom, the people descended from Esau, neighbors of Israel. God judges their pride and their attitude toward Judah. The Bible does not say with certainty who those allies were; some think of neighboring peoples, and scholars debate it.

For today: trust in alliances, power, or one's own cleverness can fail. Take care of your relationships with wisdom and humility, and place your ultimate security in God, not in people or in your own understanding.
exp.0:1:
God himself speaks to Edom in this verse and announces that he will make it small among the nations. "Small" means brought low, reduced in standing. "Nations" means the peoples around it. Edom, which thought itself great, will be seen as a minor thing.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Obadiah. Edom was the people descended from Esau, a neighbor of Israel, and it lived in high, rocky places that seemed impossible to attack. The verses that follow show that its pride deceived it. Many understand that the judgment came because of its attitude toward Judah, although this verse speaks mainly of its fall.

For today: let us not place our security in success, money, or position, because none of these truly protects us. We can ask God for a humble heart and trust in him, for he cares for those who come near to him with simplicity.
exp.0:2:
It says that Edom was deceived by its own pride. It lived in the clefts of the rocks, that is, in cracks and rocky shelters high in the mountains, and it felt so secure that it said in its heart, "Who can bring me down to the ground?"

God speaks through the prophet Obadiah. Edom was a neighboring people of Israel, and many connect them with the descendants of Esau. God announces judgment for their arrogance and their treatment of Israel. It is believed that Edom lived in a mountainous area that was hard to attack, although the exact historical details are debated.

For today: do not place your trust in your money, your achievements, or your position, as if these made you untouchable. Those things can fail. Ask God for a humble heart and trust in Him as your true refuge.
exp.0:13:
It says Edom should not have stood at the crossroads to cut off the fugitives of Judah, nor handed over their survivors when they were in distress. The crossroads are the places where several roads meet, an ideal spot for blocking the path of people trying to escape.

God speaks through the prophet Obadiah. Edom, a descendant of Esau, was a brother to Judah. When Jerusalem fell (the exact date is debated, though many think of the Babylonian invasion of 586 BC), Edom did not help. It took advantage and joined in the harm. God rebukes it for that betrayal.

For today: when someone close to you goes through a hard time, do not take advantage of it or rejoice in it. Instead, offer help, shelter, or a word of encouragement, the way you would want to receive it yourself.
exp.0:18:
It says that God's people will recover their land and will even take over territories of their enemies. Those from the Negev, the southern region, will possess the mountains of Esau, that is, Edom. Those from the foothills will possess the land of the Philistines. They will occupy the fields of Ephraim and Samaria in the north, and Benjamin will possess Gilead, east of the Jordan. Here, to "possess" means to take as an inheritance.

Obadiah is a prophet who announces God's judgment against Edom, which rejoiced when Jerusalem fell and did not help its brother Jacob. God speaks of a restoration: Israel, humbled, will again have its inheritance. Scholars disagree about whether it was fulfilled in part in history or whether it points to the future of God's kingdom.

For today: God does not forget those who have suffered injustice. We can wait with patience, without taking revenge, trusting that He restores and brings justice in his time.
exp.0:15:
Just as Edom drank on God's holy mountain, that is, celebrated and took advantage of the fall of Jerusalem, so all the nations will drink the cup of judgment without stopping. "They will drink and gulp it down" means they will take it in eagerly, without pause, until they are left dazed. "They will be as if they had never existed" means they will vanish completely.

God speaks through the prophet Obadiah, addressing Edom, the people descended from Esau. Edom rejoiced and took advantage when Judah was wounded, instead of helping its brother. Many understand "My holy mountain" to be Jerusalem. The "cup" is a biblical image of God's judgment. God promises justice and, after that, salvation for Zion.

For today: do not rejoice when someone falls, not even if they deserved it. Help, intercede, and leave justice in the hands of God, who sees everything and knows how to correct with righteousness.
exp.0:5:
This verse is an exclamation of astonishment. The reader is struck by how completely Esau's wealth will be taken. "Pillaged" means stripped of goods by force, and the "hidden treasures" are the possessions that were kept out of sight, believed to be safe. Yet even those will be found and carried off.

God speaks through the prophet Obadiah. Edom lived confident in its rocky mountains and believed itself unreachable. Moreover, it was hostile toward Israel, its brother people, in times of distress. God announces that this refuge will not save it. Ordinary thieves leave something behind, but this plundering would be total.

For today: no human security, neither money, fame, nor strength, can truly protect us. Place your trust in God and treat your family with kindness, especially when they are going through hardship.
exp.0:12:
What it says: God rebukes Edom for what it did when Jerusalem fell. He tells Edom that it should not have entered the gate of his people in their disaster, nor gloated over their suffering in that day, nor looted their wealth in that day. "Disaster" is the sense of the word the source uses here for ruin or destruction. "Gloat" means to take smug pleasure in someone else's trouble. "Loot" means to plunder or seize goods by force.

Context: God speaks through the prophet Obadiah. Edom, descended from Esau, was a relative of Judah, the people of Jacob. When foreign invaders attacked Jerusalem, Edom did not help; instead it rejoiced and took advantage. Scholars debate which invasion is meant, although many think of the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC.

For today: When someone we know is going through a crisis, we should not rejoice or take advantage. Better to draw near with compassion and help, even if there were conflicts between us.
exp.0:19:
The verse announces that the Israelites who have been exiled will once again possess lands. The exiles from the north will occupy the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath, a town on the coast of Phoenicia. The exiles from Jerusalem who are in Sepharad will take the cities of the Negev. Sepharad is a place whose location is uncertain; many think it could be Sardis, in Asia Minor, but there is no certainty.

Obadiah is a prophet about whom we know very little. He speaks on behalf of God after the fall of Jerusalem, when Edom, the people descended from Esau, rejoiced and took advantage of Judah's suffering. God promises justice to Edom and restoration to his scattered people.

For today: even if you feel far from home, defeated, or displaced, God has not forgotten you. Trust that he knows how to restore what has been lost, and wait patiently for his time.
exp.0:16:
It says that, while the nations face God's judgment, on Mount Zion there will be escape and salvation. That place will be holy, that is, set apart for God. And the people of Jacob, that is Israel, will reclaim what was rightfully theirs.

The prophet Obadiah speaks, announcing what the Lord revealed to him. Edom, a descendant of Esau, rejoiced and took advantage when Jerusalem fell. For this reason God promises to judge Edom and, at the same time, to restore his people. Scholars debate the exact time to which the fulfillment refers.

For today: even when evil seems to be winning, God does not forget his own. We can trust that he cares for those who take refuge in him, and avoid rejoicing when others are suffering.
exp.0:14:
This verse says that the Day of the LORD is near for all the nations, and that God will act in justice. What Edom has done to others will be done to Edom. "Recompense" means payment, or what is owed for one's actions; here it refers to the consequences of Edom's own deeds, which will return upon its own head.

The prophet Obadiah speaks, announcing a message from God against Edom. When Jerusalem was struck, Edom, a people related to Israel, did not help. It rejoiced, took advantage of the situation, and even handed over those who were fleeing. God responds by defending his people. Scholars debate which exact invasion is meant, but the central message is clear.

For today: God sees how we treat others, especially when they suffer. We can ask ourselves whom we should help instead of ignoring them or taking advantage of them, and leave justice to God instead of seeking revenge.
exp.0:20:
The verse says that deliverers will go up to Mount Zion, that is, to Jerusalem, to rule over the mountains of Esau, which is the region of Edom. Here "rule over" means governing with justice. The verse ends by saying that the kingdom will belong to the LORD, that is, to God.

Obadiah is a prophet who announces God's judgment against Edom for its pride and its violence against Judah, the brother people. The verses before it speak of the restoration of the exiles of Israel. Who the "deliverers" are is not entirely clear: some think of leaders or deliverers of Israel, others see a promise that points to the Messiah.

For today: although we sometimes see injustice that seems to prevail, the final word belongs to God. We can live with patience and hope, without taking revenge, trusting that his justice will come.
exp.0:7:
God asks, with firm certainty, whether He will not, on the day of His judgment, wipe out the wise men of Edom and the understanding that belongs to the mountains of Esau. The word that describes this is "destroy," meaning to be taken away or brought to an end. Wisdom here means the ability to make sound decisions with skill and good judgment. Edom trusted in its cleverness to keep it safe, but God says that this will not save it.

The Lord speaks through the prophet Obadiah. Edom, a descendant of Esau, the brother of Jacob, lived in mountainous places and believed it was protected. According to the book, Edom treated Israel badly in its time of trouble. Scholars disagree about the exact timing of these events, although many think of the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C.

For today: intelligence, money, or security are good gifts, but they do not replace God. Ask Him for humility to depend on Him and for compassion toward those who suffer, especially your own family.

sum.0: God announces judgment against Edom for its pride, and for rejoicing and taking advantage when its brother Judah was struck down by foreigners. The day of the LORD is coming upon the nations, and Edom will receive what it did to others. But on Mount Zion there will be deliverance, God's people will take back their land, and the kingdom will belong to the LORD.
